Newborn individuals of the waterflea Pleuroxus striatus emerge from the brood chamber at a total length of 0.044 cm [Lb = 0.044 cm], a measurement that reflects the size at which juveniles begin their filter-feeding existence in littoral freshwater habitats. At a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the time elapsed between the extrusion of the egg into the brood pouch and the release of the free-swimming neonate is approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days]. This rapid embryonic development is typical of small-bodied chydorid cladocerans and is highly sensitive to thermal conditions, with lower temperatures substantially prolonging the incubation interval. The initial body size at birth and the brief duration of embryogenesis are key traits that influence early survival, as smaller neonates face greater risks from predation and may require optimal food concentrations to sustain their growth during the vulnerable juvenile phase.

Following release from the brood chamber, juvenile Pleuroxus striatus undergo a series of instars during which they increase steadily in body length. The total length at which these sub-adult individuals first become reproductively functional, marking the completion of the juvenile phase and the onset of ovarian maturation, has been determined to be 0.065 cm [Lp = 0.065 cm]. This length is reached approximately 12 days after birth [tp = approximately 12 days after birth] when the animals are maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. The attainment of this critical size is a prerequisite for the development of the first clutch of parthenogenetic eggs. The consistency of this value within controlled laboratory conditions suggests that a threshold body length, rather than a fixed chronological age independent of size, serves as the primary trigger for the pubertal molt in this species.

A reproductively mature female Pleuroxus striatus at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] deposits a single clutch of parthenogenetic eggs into the dorsal brood chamber immediately following each adult molt. The frequency of these reproductive events is tightly linked to the molting interval, and over the entire adult lifespan, which spans roughly 77 days [am = roughly 77 days], a female can produce up to approximately 20 separate clutches at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. From the total of roughly 20 molting events over the adult lifespan, the mean interval between successive clutches is approximately 3.3 days, producing a sustained daily output of roughly 0.31 offspring per day per female [Ri = roughly 0.31 offspring per day per female] that drives the species' rapid population dynamics under stable thermal conditions. The sustained production of clutches at this thermal optimum underscores the efficiency of the parthenogenetic reproductive mode characteristic of the Chydoridae, allowing for exponential population growth in ephemeral or productive habitats.

Application of an established length–dry weight regression for chydorid cladocerans, specifically the relationship described by Culver and Boucherle for a morphologically similar species, yields an estimated ultimate dry weight of 6.6 micrograms  for an individual Pleuroxus striatus that has reached its maximum body length. The maximum body length itself, representing the final size attained by a fully mature adult after the cessation of molting, is 0.090 cm [Li = 0.090 cm]. This asymptotic length is rarely achieved under natural conditions where predation and resource limitation truncate the lifespan. The relationship between body length and dry mass in these small branchiopods is typically allometric, with mass increasing proportionally faster than length, so that a female nearing the ultimate length carries considerably more tissue mass than a female at the pubertal size threshold.

Total lifespan in Pleuroxus striatus at a constant laboratory temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] has been recorded as 77 days [am = 77 days], with mortality increasing markedly after the cessation of reproductive output. The age at birth of 2 days [ab = 2 days] and the time to puberty of 12 days [tp = 12 days] together produce a life history pattern characterized by an early and intense reproductive effort, typical of r-selected chydorid cladocerans adapted to ephemeral freshwater habitats where maximizing fitness under uncertain environmental conditions is paramount at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C] at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This demographic schedule is consistent with the r-selected strategy observed in many small cladocerans inhabiting temporary or unpredictable aquatic environments.
